title.en: The Roman conquest of Hispania

records.anchorText: Emporion, Tarraco, Carthago Nova, Numantia and the Cantabrian mountains

en: The Atlas opens in 218 BCE, when Roman forces landed at Emporion during the Second Punic War. This marks the opening of Roman conquest and the start of the Atlas’s Hispanic civilizational chronology, rather than the immediate establishment of a unified Roman province.

Carthago Nova fell to Scipio in 209 BCE, and the conflict with Carthage gave way to struggles against multiple Iberian powers. The Lusitanian wars and the resistance of Viriathus, the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE, and the Augustan wars in the northwest belong to distinct theatres and generations.

Conquest established the basis for extending Roman law, Latin and urban institutions unevenly across the peninsula. Mediterranean ports and inland roads enabled the movement of troops, minerals, agricultural products and ideas. Over time these networks made Hispania a Roman political and cultural space from which later Hispanic and Lusophone institutions inherited much.

Open playback with the 218 BCE coastal arrival, not a filled modern peninsula. Add Carthago Nova, the Lusitanian campaigns, Numantia and Augustus’s Cantabrian–Asturian wars as dated child actions. Link territorial gains separately to provincial organization and later civic incorporation.

title.en: Roman Hispania: provinces, cities, law, and Christian networks

records.anchorText: Tarraco, Corduba, Emerita Augusta, Bracara Augusta and Carthago Nova

en: Rome created Hispania Citerior and Ulterior in 197 BCE while conquest was still under way. The Augustan settlement reorganized much of the peninsula into Tarraconensis, Baetica and Lusitania; later imperial reforms produced subdivisions including Gallaecia and Carthaginiensis.

Roads and ports connected mountains, mines, agricultural districts and provincial capitals. The Roman cities of Bracara and Emerita became administrative anchors, but the province of Lusitania did not have the borders of modern Portugal; neither did Roman Gallaecia coincide with the present autonomous community.

Latin spread through military, civic and commercial life and furnished the linguistic inheritance from which Iberian Romance languages developed. Christianity took root in late Roman urban communities; the early Council of Elvira is evidence of ecclesiastical organization, though the precise year remains debated.

Show dated provincial seats, road segments and evidence-based boundary intervals. Keep Roman municipal law, ecclesiastical geography and economy distinct. This is a Roman Iberian foundation for the Atlas, not an assertion that Spain and Portugal already existed.

title.en: Suevic Gallaecia and the Visigothic kingdom of Toledo

records.anchorText: Braga, Mérida, Toledo, Cartagena and the Byzantine southeastern coast

en: Suevic control developed in the northwest after the early fifth-century movements into Hispania. Braga became a religious and political center with a history distinct from Toledo. The Suevic kingdom was conquered by Leovigild in 585, and should remain distinguishable on the map until its incorporation.

Visigothic authority also competed with Byzantine Spania along portions of the southern and southeastern coast. That contest, and the independent history of the northwest, make a single uninterrupted fifth-century Visigothic peninsula misleading.

Recared’s profession of Catholicism at the Third Council of Toledo in 589 marked a decisive institutional alignment. The councils and later Liber Iudiciorum show how monarchy, Church and law used different instruments to shape a common polity.

Give Suevic, Visigothic and Byzantine seats separate validity intervals. Mark the council and later legal codification as institutions rather than new borders; early migration reports must not become sharp territorial polygons.

title.en: Guadalete, the conquest of Hispania and the political cycles of al-Andalus

records.anchorText: Strait of Gibraltar → Guadalete region → Toledo, Córdoba and Zaragoza

en: Ṭāriq ibn Ziyād crossed the Strait in 711 and defeated the forces of King Roderic. The site of the battle conventionally called Guadalete is disputed. Umayyad commanders then advanced by warfare and negotiated submission; the agreement associated with Theodemir illustrates an alternative to occupation by battle.

The seizure of centers including Toledo produced political rupture, while some local structures and communities persisted. The independent emirate established at Córdoba in 756, the caliphate proclaimed in 929 and its dissolution in 1031 were three different state changes.

Córdoba’s power rested on revenue, irrigated agriculture, urban craft and long-distance networks. Warfare with Christian states was recurrent, but trade, diplomacy and local agreement crossed frontiers. Almanzor’s later raids, including Santiago in 997, are expedition records rather than permanent conquests.

Represent crossing, battles, pact zones and regime changes independently. Place the disputed battlefield schematically and show the emirate, caliphate, frontier commands and ensuing taifas in distinct time slices.

title.en: Covadonga, Oviedo and the making of Asturias

records.anchorText: Cangas de Onís, Covadonga, Oviedo, Santiago de Compostela and the Duero approaches

en: A Christian political nucleus formed among the Cantabrian mountains after the fall of the Visigothic monarchy. Covadonga is its symbolic episode; the date usually assigned to it and the size and nature of the encounter should be marked as uncertain.

Under Alfonso II and Alfonso III the kings built a court and ecclesiastical center around Oviedo and extended their sphere toward Galicia and the Duero. Later chronicles articulated Visigothic continuity, a claim that should be read alongside new institutions and circumstances.

Bueno understands Asturias’s expansion as an answer to the challenge from al-Andalus, which could not be met by remaining enclosed in the mountains. Insua develops the Asturian–Leonese sequence as a political process rather than dating the completed Spanish nation to Covadonga.

Merge this as an expansion of editorial #1. Plot the sequence of royal seats, churches and roads; distinguish the date of the event from the date and political perspective of its chronicle. Link the shift toward León to a child record.

title.en: Pamplona and Navarre: a Pyrenean kingdom takes shape

records.anchorText: Roncesvalles, Pamplona, Nájera, Viguera and the western Pyrenees

en: Roncesvalles in 778 belongs to a history of Frankish intervention and local resistance; it does not itself establish the borders of a kingdom. Pamplona’s ninth-century monarchy arose through regional forces and changing relationships with Franks, Córdoba and the Ebro valley.

Sancho III’s reach in the early eleventh century linked counties and kingdoms through kinship and temporary authority. It did not turn all lands associated with him into Navarre. Viguera’s short-lived tenth-century subkingdom illustrates why a dynastic appanage needs its own status and validity.

In 1076 Pamplona and Aragón came under the same king, with other lands passing to Castilian-Leonese rule. After Alfonso I’s death in 1134 the Pamplonese restored a separate line under García Ramírez; the name Navarre took hold later in the century.

Animate the fortified passes, royal seats and actual dynastic changes. Use separate relations for shared monarch, vassalage, appanage and direct rule. Do not flatten Pamplona, Viguera or later Navarre into present provincial outlines.

title.en: Barcelona and the Catalan counties: from Carolingian frontiers to the Crown of Aragón

records.anchorText: Girona, Barcelona, Urgell, Cerdanya, Besalú and Corbeil

en: Girona and Barcelona came under Frankish authority in the late eighth and early ninth centuries. Multiple counties formed along the frontier; Barcelona’s eventual prominence was not the starting condition, and the practical ties to the Frankish monarchy loosened over time.

The political relationship agreed in 1137 between Petronila of Aragón and Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona brought dynastic union. It preserved Aragón as a kingdom and the Catalan territories as a distinct political and legal component.

The 1258 Treaty of Corbeil addressed claims on both sides of the Pyrenees. County succession, Catalan legal institutions and trans-Pyrenean interests developed at different speeds; Urgell, in particular, should not be erased early from the county layer.

Show Girona and Barcelona as dated events, then changes in the individual counties. The Crown of Aragón must have constituent relationships rather than a solid color granting one component the institutions of the others.

title.en: Aragón, Sobrarbe and Ribagorza: from counties to a kingdom

records.anchorText: Jaca, Huesca, Barbastro, Zaragoza and the upper Ebro

en: The Pyrenean county of Aragón grew amid shifting influence from Pamplona and the Franks. Sobrarbe and Ribagorza had distinct political histories, and their incorporation should not be backdated to an undifferentiated Aragonese origin.

Ramiro I’s eleventh-century rule marked a new dynastic center. Peter I defeated opposing forces at Alcoraz in 1096 and took Huesca; Alfonso I captured Zaragoza in 1118 and established control over key parts of the Ebro system.

The Ebro’s towns and irrigation networks altered the kingdom’s resources and relations with Muslim, Christian and Jewish communities. Repopulation, charters and military authority need locally sourced dates.
Keep Jaca and Zaragoza as dated seats. Give Huesca and the later dynastic union with Barcelona separate events; the Atlas should not label all northeastern territories as the Kingdom of Aragón.

title.en: Portucale becomes Portugal: São Mamede, Zamora and papal recognition

records.anchorText: Porto, Coimbra, Guimarães, Ourique, Zamora and Lisbon

en: The county tradition associated with Portucale and later the frontier around Coimbra preceded the county governed by Henry of Burgundy and Teresa. These were not the same territorial snapshot and neither was yet the later sovereign Portuguese kingdom.

Afonso Henriques prevailed at São Mamede in 1128, fought at Ourique in 1139 and reached the Zamora settlement with Alfonso VII in 1143. Pope Alexander III’s Manifestis Probatum in 1179 has its own place in the sequence of recognition; Ourique’s later foundation legend belongs to a different evidence layer.

Santarém and Lisbon fell in 1147; the siege of Lisbon involved northern European crusaders as well as Portuguese forces. The Tagus became a major route for provisioning, emigration, trade and royal administration.

Expand editorial #2 rather than replacing Zamora with an oversimplified independence date. Plot the two county phases, São Mamede, Lisbon and the successive recognition instruments. Carry southern expansion through to the independent Algarve sequence.

title.en: León and Galicia: royal succession, Compostela and union under Ferdinand III

records.anchorText: León, Santiago de Compostela, Braga and the Duero frontier

en: The early tenth-century shift of the political center to León followed Asturian expansion. The León-based monarchy encompassed territories with distinct elites and ecclesiastical centers; Galicia should remain legible within these changing arrangements.

The partitions of royal inheritance produced moments of separate kingship: García received Galicia in 1065 and lost power during the struggles among Ferdinand I’s heirs. These changes should be traced against León and Castile rather than expressed as continuous modern national borders.

Compostela developed as an ecclesiastical and pilgrimage center, linked to exchange beyond the kingdom. The Cortes at León in 1188 belong on an institutional track, while the 1230 succession placed the Castilian and Leonese crowns definitively under Ferdinand III.

Keep Galicia and León independently identifiable after personal or dynastic consolidation. Use dated claims and governance evidence to show partitions; distinguish Galicia as a kingdom and title from an always independent state.

title.en: Castile: county, crown and the Toledo frontier

records.anchorText: Burgos, the Duero, Toledo, Uclés and León

en: Castile grew out of a group of frontier counties. Fernán González consolidated power in the tenth century; later changes under the descendants of Sancho III and Ferdinand I do not fit one simple declaration of independence.

After the succession partition of 1065, Sancho II held Castile. Alfonso VI reunified several inheritances and took Toledo in 1085. Its history as an Andalusi taifa, then as a Castilian kingdom and ecclesiastical center, must stay visible.

Almoravid victories at Sagrajas in 1086 and Uclés in 1108 checked the pace of expansion. Toledo also became a center for translation and intellectual exchange, in changing arrangements involving Latin, Romance, Arabic and Jewish scholarship.

Show Burgos and Toledo as separate nodes, and map frontiers rather than definite lines where settlement and allegiance varied. The 1230 union enlarged a composite crown; it did not convert all constituent kingdoms into the old county of Castile.

title.en: Taifas, the Portuguese southern frontier and the military orders

records.anchorText: Zaragoza, Toledo, Badajoz, Seville, Silves, Alcácer do Sal and Faro

en: The end of the Córdoba caliphate left competing taifa kingdoms. Zaragoza, Toledo, Badajoz and Seville had different spheres of power; smaller centers such as Niebla, Silves, Murcia and the Balearics entered successive taifa and North African arrangements.

In western Iberia the advancing Portuguese monarchy faced different rivals at different times. The success at Santarém and Lisbon in 1147 did not secure the Alentejo and Algarve, and the Portuguese capture of Silves in 1189 was reversed by Almohad power in 1191.

The conquest of Alcácer do Sal in 1217 and later campaigns into the Algarve extended Portuguese territory. Military orders, municipalities and royal grants gave the frontier institutions that lasted beyond the campaigns.

Show major taifas as dated individual states, then distinguish Almoravid and Almohad phases and later successor entities. On the Portuguese track, use capture, loss and recovery events rather than a permanently advancing line.

title.en: Almoravids, Almohads and the campaign of Las Navas de Tolosa

records.anchorText: Toledo, Sagrajas, Uclés, Alarcos and Las Navas de Tolosa

en: The fall of Toledo prompted intervention by the Almoravids from North Africa, whose victory at Sagrajas in 1086 checked Alfonso VI. Their rule over Iberian territories was not the same as the earlier taifa system.

The Almohads later took over much of the region and defeated Alfonso VIII of Castile at Alarcos in 1195. The battle and the resulting balance of power should be shown separately from wider North African chronology.

In 1212 a coalition led by the kings of Castile, Aragón and Navarre defeated the Almohad army at Las Navas de Tolosa. Papal support and military orders situate the campaign within the history of crusade; participation did not abolish the rival agendas of the Iberian crowns.
Plot passages and battles, with no instant change over all of al-Andalus. Add the later Christian conquests and the emergence of Nasrid Granada through independently dated events.

title.en: Iberian partitions, Muret and the shift toward the Mediterranean

records.anchorText: Tudilén, Cuenca, Cazola, Muret, Almizra and Corbeil

en: Tudilén in 1151 and Cazola in 1179 regulated Castilian and Aragonese expectations about further conquest. Alfonso VIII’s seizure of Cuenca in 1177 illustrates how actual occupation had a trajectory that cannot be read from agreements alone.

Peter II of Aragón was killed at Muret in 1213 while supporting his allies against the Albigensian Crusade. This defeat checked the Crown’s influence north of the Pyrenees but did not settle every Catalan and Aragonese interest in Occitania.

Almizra in 1244 defined areas of expansion between Castile and Aragón in the southeast, while the 1258 Treaty of Corbeil dealt with French and Aragonese claims. Distinguish the crown’s peninsular bargaining from its different choices in France and at sea.

Build these instruments as dated diplomatic actions with precise scope and sources. Add Muret as a battle with identifiable actors and no automatic perimeter change; use the later Valencia, Murcia and Catalan records for actual jurisdictional updates.

title.en: Navarre between Iberia and France: frontier losses and the Évreux kings

records.anchorText: Pamplona, Olite, Vitoria-Gasteiz, Bayonne, Paris and Cocherel

en: The struggle around 1199–1200 transferred key western territories from Navarre into the Castilian sphere, including Álava and Gipuzkoa in changing arrangements. Biscay’s lordship and later tie to the Castilian crown need their own history; none of the three is an interchangeable province from the start.
In 1234 a Champagne line succeeded in Navarre. Ties with the French crown deepened under Joan I and Philip IV, before Joan II and Philip of Évreux began a new Navarrese succession in 1328.

Charles II’s dynastic stakes drew Navarre into the French conflicts of the fourteenth century, including the defeat of his forces at Cocherel in 1364. Charles III, king from 1387, pursued a different policy, with Olite gaining importance as a court center.

Record actual Pyrenean possessions, noncontiguous French interests and alliances separately. Put the 1328 separation in the dynastic view. Do not map a single uninterrupted French occupation of Navarre.

title.en: Mallorca, Valencia and Murcia: three kingdoms and their frontier settlements

records.anchorText: Palma, Ibiza, Menorca, Valencia, Alicante, Orihuela and Murcia

en: James I took Mallorca from 1229 and Valencia in 1238. The resulting kingdoms obtained different legal arrangements and population histories; Mallorca became the center of a separate dynastic branch after 1276. Ibiza and Menorca require their own dates.

Murcia’s negotiated submission in 1243 brought much of it into the Castilian sphere; revolt and campaigning in the 1260s required intervention by James I on behalf of Alfonso X. That intervention did not make all Murcia permanently Aragonese.

Torrellas in 1304 and Elche in 1305 divided claims in the southeast. Orihuela and Alicante entered the Valencian sphere, while the city and much of the kingdom of Murcia remained Castilian. Commercial ports and agricultural systems crossed the legal line.

Build Mallorca, Valencia and Murcia as separate entities, including enclaves and transition intervals. Record the treaty-based changes and later on-the-ground delimitations rather than filling by present regional borders.

title.en: Castile–León, Andalusia and the Portuguese Algarve

records.anchorText: León, Córdoba, Jaén, Seville, Niebla, Faro and Badajoz

en: Ferdinand III inherited León in 1230 after already holding Castile. Córdoba followed in 1236, Jaén in 1246 and Seville in 1248. Those conquests changed royal revenues, river access and settlement; distinct kingdoms and jurisdictions persisted in the broader crown.

Portugal consolidated control in the Algarve by 1249. Castilian claims persisted until the 1267 Treaty of Badajoz; acquisition and recognition must therefore be dated separately. Niebla, conquered for Castile in 1262, was a separate holdout and later lordship.

The Guadalquivir and Guadiana regions show how ports, castles, military orders, municipal privileges and ecclesiastical organization worked together but occupied unequal territories. Commercial traffic fostered Atlantic ties without erasing internal legal boundaries.

Extend editorial #3 with event-level nodes, including the Christian kingdoms of Córdoba, Jaén and Seville and the Portuguese title of the Algarve. Keep Toledo, León, Galicia, Murcia and earlier titles available in the legal and dynastic layer.

title.en: Nasrid Granada: state formation, tribute, diplomacy and the last Iberian war

records.anchorText: Arjona, Granada, Málaga, Almería, Loja, Baza and Santa Fe

en: Muḥammad I established Nasrid power in the 1230s and made Granada its center. The 1246 accommodation with Ferdinand III involved tribute and a relationship of dependence, but left an emirate able to negotiate, govern and fight.

Trade and urban craft connected Granada to the Mediterranean and Maghreb. Its frontier was a dynamic zone of castles, exchanges, raids and diplomacy; Nasrid interests did not invariably coincide with those of Marinid or other Muslim rulers.

In the war of 1482–1492, defeats and captures at places including Málaga and Baza opened the way to the capitulations of 1491 and entry into Granada in January 1492. The surrender terms and their implementation, later coercive conversion and the Morisco question have distinct chronologies.

Expand existing editorial #8 and create child records for Nasrid formation, contested frontiers, the 1482–1492 campaign and entry into Granada. Show mercantile connections separately from sovereignty and do not conflate the end of the emirate with the departure of all Muslims.

title.en: Badajoz and Alcañices: the Luso-Castilian frontier

records.anchorText: Badajoz, the Guadiana, Riba-Côa, Olivenza and Alcañices

en: Portugal’s conquest of the Algarve preceded Castile’s settlement of the jurisdictional dispute. The 1267 Treaty of Badajoz clarified this southern theatre; it did not itself settle the whole border.

On 12 September 1297 Dinis and Fernando IV’s Castile reached a settlement at Alcañices. The exchange and recognition of specific places, including the Riba-Côa area and Olivenza, stabilized important stretches between two already distinct monarchies.

The frontier remained a lived region of trade, fortification and settlement. Neither treaty drew every modern segment to survey precision, and later territorial changes such as the Olivenza issue must be dated to their own instruments and occupations.

Add separate title change events for 1267 and 1297 with the forts or sites named in the treaty. Draw surveyed segments only from supporting cartography and maintain open geometry where no source justifies a precise line.

title.en: The Battle for the Strait: Tarifa, Gibraltar, Río Salado and Algeciras

records.anchorText: Tarifa, Gibraltar, Algeciras, Ceuta and the crossing to the Maghreb

en: Marinid interventions from North Africa changed the balance at the Strait in the late thirteenth century. Castile took Tarifa in 1292 and held it against a later siege; the positions of Nasrid Granada and Marinid Morocco changed over time.

Castile seized Gibraltar in 1309 and lost it to the Marinids in 1333. In 1340 Alfonso XI of Castile and Afonso IV of Portugal defeated a Marinid–Nasrid coalition near Tarifa at Río Salado. That victory checked large-scale Marinid intervention without instantly ending Muslim rule at every port.

Algeciras fell to Alfonso XI in 1344, and his renewed Gibraltar campaign ended with his death in 1350. Later Nasrid occupation and the Castilian capture of Gibraltar in 1462 belong to distinct records. Ports controlled provisioning and crossings as well as commerce between the Mediterranean and Atlantic.

Make this a multi-part playback track. The day or month of a port transfer must come from that port’s evidence; display the defeat of an army separately from the new jurisdiction and effective occupation of each fortress.

title.en: The Kingdom of Mallorca, Aragonese reunion and Llucmajor

records.anchorText: Palma, Perpignan, Montpellier, Roussillon and Cerdanya

en: The inheritance of James I made Mallorca the center of a junior royal branch with mainland possessions. Perpignan mattered to the court as did Palma, and the kingdom’s territories did not form a continuous island unit.

Relations with the ruling line in Aragón involved dependency, conflict and negotiation. Peter IV took Mallorca in 1343 and gained control of Roussillon and Cerdanya; James III’s attempt to return ended at Llucmajor in 1349.

Mallorca’s ports, credit and seafaring linked western Mediterranean markets to Atlantic ventures. Reincorporation changed the sovereign while preserving a distinct kingdom and institutions; Montpellier had a separate trajectory.

Plot island, mainland and seaborne links separately. Display the 1343–1349 military sequence with dates for individual territories, and distinguish loss of the independent ruling branch from abolition of the kingdom.

title.en: The Crown of Aragón across the western Mediterranean

records.anchorText: Palermo, Barcelona, Cagliari and Alghero; Naples as a later branch

en: The Sicilian Vespers in 1282 brought Peter III of Aragón into the war over Sicily. The ensuing conflict with the Angevins and France was wider than the island; the French invasion of Aragón’s lands in 1285 is a separate land and naval sequence.

Anagni in 1295 and Caltabellotta in 1302 did not produce a single uniform Mediterranean crown. The latter settled the immediate conflict around the insular kingdom under Frederick; show changing dynastic links and the distinction between Sicily and the mainland kingdom later commonly called Naples.

Sardinian campaigns beginning in 1323 created another contested front, and the Crown faced local powers and Genoese rivals. Merchants, consulates and fleets spanned a much wider world than any of these possessions.

Add named battles, treaties and port occupations before drawing any sovereignty change. Show dynastic links to Sicily and specific Sardinian footholds independently; give Barcelona’s commercial connections a separate network layer.

title.en: Dinis consolidates the Portuguese kingdom: university, frontier and the Order of Christ

records.anchorText: Lisbon, Coimbra, Alcañices, the Algarve and Castro Marim

en: Dinis’s reign combined frontier stabilization with changes in royal government. A studium was established in 1290; the institution moved between Lisbon and Coimbra over the following centuries, so its first location and later home require different records.

Settlement charters and local administration strengthened parts of the border. The Treaty of Alcañices with Castile concerned specified places and claims; durable jurisdiction also required institutions and people in those localities.

In 1319 the Order of Christ was established after the suppression of the Templars. Its properties and obligations belong to a documented institutional history. Its later Atlantic role should not be projected backward to the date of its creation.

Plot the university’s relocations, the frontier places documented in Alcañices and the order’s separately dated seats. Connect the institution to later Atlantic expeditions only when a specific patron, grant or voyage supports the link.

title.en: Plague, the Aragonese Unions and the War of the Two Peters

records.anchorText: Épila, Valencia, Tarazona, Calatayud and the frontier with Castile

en: The Black Death and clashes over the privileges of the Aragonese and Valencian Unions put Peter IV’s authority under pressure. His victory at Épila in 1348 and suppression of the Valencian Union closed particular political confrontations without erasing the crown’s constituent laws.

The war between Peter IV of Aragón and Peter I of Castile began in 1356. Its forces contested towns and communications on both sides of the frontier, and its alliances became entangled with the Castilian succession struggle.

Temporary treaties did not end the conflict; the 1375 Peace of Almazán concluded it. Campaigns and plague damaged commerce and settlement, while maritime resources and negotiations helped the crowns sustain war.

Show Épila, identifiable occupations and settlements as separate actions. End military control spells with the correct local evidence rather than treating the declared peace date as proof of every handover.

title.en: Castilian civil war: Nájera, Montiel and the Trastámara dynasty

records.anchorText: Burgos, Nájera, Montiel and Carmona

en: Peter I and his half-brother Henry of Trastámara fought for the Castilian crown. Conflicts over patronage and succession drew in towns and nobles with different interests. The English alliance with Peter and French support for Henry linked the struggle to the Hundred Years’ War.

Peter and the Black Prince defeated Henry’s forces at Nájera in 1367, but the victory failed to establish a lasting settlement. Henry returned, and Peter’s death after the battle of Montiel in 1369 opened a new dynastic phase.

Resistance and consolidation continued beyond Montiel, including the fall of Carmona in 1371. Fiscal strains and rewards to supporters reshaped royal power; an instant national recoloring at one battle would miss both the struggle and its outcome.
Plot the armies, city-held intervals and the dynastic change separately. Keep Portuguese and Aragonese interventions as connected tracks, not as interchangeable sides of the Castilian war.

title.en: The Fernandine Wars and Portugal’s disputed succession

records.anchorText: Lisbon, Galicia, Alcoutim and Salvaterra de Magos

en: After Peter I’s death, Fernando I of Portugal advanced claims to the Castilian crown. The Fernandine Wars brought repeated confrontation and alternating diplomacy, including operations involving Galicia.

The wars did not make all supporters of Fernando part of Portugal. Treaties at Alcoutim and Santarém mark phases of the conflict, while Ferdinand’s alliances with England and his later settlement with Castile served different needs.

In 1383 the marriage arrangements of Beatriz and Juan I of Castile at Salvaterra de Magos attempted to manage succession and Portuguese autonomy. Fernando’s death later that year brought the issue into open conflict.
Link campaigns to the dynastic claim and dated instruments; never draw claimed Castile as Portuguese administered territory. Link Beatriz’s and the Master of Avis’s claims to the following crisis.

title.en: The Catalan Atlas and the charted Atlantic before the Canary conquest

records.anchorText: Mallorca, western Mediterranean, eastern Atlantic and northwestern Africa

en: The Catalan Atlas, associated with the Cresques workshop on Mallorca and conventionally dated around 1375, brings portolan practice into conversation with courtly, geographic and commercial knowledge. Nearby coasts and remote regions are represented through different sources.

The atlas depicts routes and distant powers without implying first-hand voyage coverage of everything shown. Mediterranean, trans-Saharan and Atlantic information traveled through merchants, sailors, interpreters and manuscript workshops.

European charts and expeditions recorded Atlantic islands before regular occupation. The Norman-led expedition under Castilian auspices beginning in 1402 marks a different milestone: conquest and settlement in the Canaries, whose island-by-island path belongs to A09.

Add a 1375 knowledge snapshot with asset provenance. End a line at the extent actually represented; do not shade all of Africa as surveyed. Show the first Canary campaign separately from earlier charts, claims and reports.

title.en: Avis and Portuguese independence: Lisbon, Aljubarrota and Windsor

records.anchorText: Lisbon, Atoleiros, Coimbra, Aljubarrota, Valverde and Windsor

en: Fernando’s death opened a succession crisis involving Beatriz’s supporters and those of the Master of Avis. Lisbon resisted siege in 1384; Atoleiros was a separate field victory that year. The Cortes of Coimbra acclaimed João I in 1385.

At Aljubarrota in August 1385 the Portuguese forces defeated Juan I’s invading army. The battle at Trancoso that year was a separate Portuguese victory. Nuno Álvares Pereira’s campaigns included Valverde later in 1385. These victories established a basis for Avis rule, while local loyalties and formal recognition changed on different schedules.

The Treaty of Windsor in 1386 strengthened the English relationship, following earlier Anglo-Portuguese arrangements. The 1411 peace with Castile belongs to a separate legal stage. Political consolidation strengthened the dynasty that would launch the Ceuta expedition in 1415.

Plot Lisbon’s siege, Coimbra, Aljubarrota and other battles as separate operations; keep royal election, English alliance and Castilian peace as distinct documents. Do not turn the victory into a modern border redraw.

title.en: The late Trastámara settlement and urban crisis in Castile and Aragón

records.anchorText: Bayonne, Palencia, Seville, Córdoba, Valencia, Barcelona and Mallorca

en: The 1388 Bayonne agreement resolved John of Gaunt’s claim to Castile through a settlement linked to the marriage of Catherine of Lancaster and the future Henry III. This is a different outcome from the 1385 Portuguese victory.

In 1391 attacks on Jewish communities began in Seville and spread through cities in Castile and the Crown of Aragón. The effects included death, migration and conversion. The geography must be built from evidence city by city rather than treated as one simultaneous national event.

Henry III’s consolidation and the turn toward Atlantic projects unfolded amid these urban and dynastic tensions. The 1402 expedition to the Canaries began under Castilian auspices, but its early character was seigneurial rather than a single crown campaign taking all the islands.

Add Bayonne as a dynastic instrument, and use dated and carefully sourced local records for 1391. Cross-link the 1402 expedition to A09 so that a political transition in Iberia and conquest in the Atlantic remain distinct.

title.en: Conquest of the Canaries and Atlantic staging

records.anchorText: Lanzarote → Gran Canaria → La Palma → Tenerife

en: The conquest began with lordly expeditions and continued through royal campaigns. Island Indigenous societies did not form a single polity; outcomes and chronologies varied.
Fortified settlements and Atlantic sailing supplied a bridge between Iberia and later crossings. Sugar cultivation, migration and coerced Indigenous labor gave the islands a role beyond resupply.
Gran Canaria, La Palma and Tenerife were conquered in distinct campaigns, with Tenerife’s defeat in 1496. Survivors entered a society marked by both dispossession and cultural continuity.
Show each island separately and retain Indigenous presence after annexation. Mark known chart appearances before conquest, then landings, fighting and the growth of ports as separate operations.

title.en: Caspe, Catalan civil war and the dynastic convergence of the crowns

records.anchorText: Caspe, Balaguer, Barcelona, Segovia, Toro and Pamplona

en: Martin I’s death triggered a succession crisis in the Crown of Aragón. The Compromise of Caspe selected Ferdinand of Antequera in 1412, and resistance centered on the count of Urgell was defeated in 1413. A Trastámara monarch did not erase the Crown’s constitutional plurality.

The Catalan Civil War of 1462–1472 challenged John II’s rule. Separately, the Castilian succession war followed Isabella’s accession, involving Portugal and rival claims on behalf of Juana. Toro in 1476 and the 1479 Alcáçovas settlement provided distinct military and diplomatic turning points.

Isabella and Ferdinand had married in 1469; their dynastic convergence became effective across both crowns in 1479. Castilian forces seized Upper Navarre in 1512 and it was incorporated into the Crown of Castile in 1515 while retaining institutions; Lower Navarre followed a separate trajectory.

Keep marriage, campaign, accession and recognized settlement separate, and leave Portugal independent. Use dated Navarre features north and south of the Pyrenees; maintain Aragonese, Catalan, Valencian and Castilian institutions under a common dynasty.

title.en: Ceuta to Calicut: Portugal’s southern route and the Islamic powers

records.anchorText: Ceuta, Tangier, Cape Bojador, Cape of Good Hope, Mozambique and Calicut

en: The Avis monarchy captured Ceuta in 1415, but the 1437 Tangier expedition failed. The monarchy subsequently seized Alcácer Ceguer, and took Arzila and occupied Tangier in 1471. Morocco was an active set of powers and markets rather than a shore waiting for expansion.

Island settlement, trade in gold and captives, and Atlantic wind knowledge supported the exploration of Africa’s coast. Dias rounded the southern cape in 1488; Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 through a sea already navigated by African, Arab, Gujarati and other mariners.

Portugal’s African and Indian Ocean axis combined royal strategy, crusading aims, commerce and local diplomacy. It took shape before the major Ottoman conquests in Syria and Egypt; Mamluk, Moroccan and Ottoman interests must not be collapsed into one empire.

Link the existing Ceuta, Dias and da Gama cards with dated stops and a paired comparison with Castile’s western plan. Do not depict the route as a proven Portuguese operation to encircle the Ottoman state.

title.en: Madeira, the Azores and Cabo Verde

records.anchorText: Porto Santo, Funchal, Azores, Santiago

en: Portuguese Atlantic island colonization proceeded in stages. The conventional years of reported discovery, crown grants and permanent settlement are often different, and some priority claims are contested.
Madeira’s sugar and the Azores’ agriculture served different markets. Atlantic island routes drew on pilots’ knowledge of winds and the ocean return arc.

Cabo Verde’s Santiago grew as a commercial center linking Africa, Europe and the Atlantic trade in enslaved people. The islands became sites of Creole cultural formation, rather than mere waypoints toward America.
Add island-specific observations and settlement nodes. Use the Cantino planisphere as a later knowledge snapshot and attach separate evidence to each early date.

title.en: Bojador, Elmina, Kongo and the southern cape

records.anchorText: Bojador → Elmina → Congo mouth → Cape route

en: Gil Eanes’s passage beyond Bojador in 1434 belongs to a sequence of Atlantic voyages, not to a sudden discovery of the African coast. Elmina’s fort in 1482 depended on negotiations and access to an existing gold trade.
Diogo Cão reached the Congo River mouth during voyages of the 1480s, while Dias rounded southern Africa in 1488. Neither event established Portuguese rule inland.
Relations with Kongo developed through diplomacy, missionaries and commerce, including the increasingly disruptive trade in captives. Kongo remained an actor with its own institutions and rulers.
Split the route at documented stops. Attach forts and Christian diplomacy to their own dates, and retain the existing Dias record without lighting the African interior.

title.en: Constantinople, Granada and the westward approach to Asia

records.anchorText: Constantinople, Granada, Santa Fe, Palos and a conjectural route to Asian destinations
unresolved: a conjectural route to Asian destinations

en: Ottoman forces took Constantinople in 1453. Their expansion altered the strategic setting of Mediterranean Christendom, but Italian, Ottoman and other traders continued to exchange goods. The Cape and westward schemes must not be explained as reactions to a total closure of trade.

Bueno reads the long Iberian struggle to prevail over Islamic political powers as a formative process. In his reading the Catholic Monarchs pursued a westward route to Asia that could reach the Ottoman strategic rear, extending the old peninsular confrontation into a project on the scale of the globe.

The 1492 capitulations at Santa Fe and Columbus’s recorded interest in the Indies disclose a royal charter, titles and commercial expectations; the prologue to the voyage journal also links Granada and the embassy to the Great Khan. These are documentary anchors. A formal anti-Ottoman military directive is not stated in the Santa Fe instrument.

Render Constantinople and Granada as dated historical facts, the planned westward approach as a conjectural destination layer, and the actual track ending in the Caribbean as a different layer. Label the geopolitical connection as Bueno’s interpretation. Do not draw an expedition arriving in Asia in 1492.

title.en: The Columbian crossings and Tordesillas as three different map operations

records.anchorText: Palos, Canary Islands, Guanahaní/Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, Tordesillas

en: The first crossing attempted to reach the Indies by sailing west and instead linked Castilian pilots to Caribbean communities. The Atlas introduces local guides, toponyms and routes here and in subsequent encounter records, timed to when they entered the documentary record. The identification of Guanahaní remains disputed, so a route may end in the Bahamas without silently fixing one island as certain.

The second voyage carried a much larger fleet and settlement personnel. Landfalls in the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico added new observations; La Isabela began a settlement process with its own timeline.

Tordesillas set out a line 370 leagues west of the Cabo Verde islands, but longitude, the baseline and league length complicated practical definition. The treaty was an agreement between crowns rather than a survey or grant of Indigenous consent.

title.en: Nebrija, Camões and languages across the oceans

records.anchorText: Salamanca and Lisbon; publication and translation networks

en: Nebrija’s 1492 grammar addressed Castilian as a language that could be systematically described and taught. It can be read alongside the emerging use of vernaculars in political institutions and printing.

Portuguese writers developed their own traditions of codification and cosmography. Camões’s Os Lusíadas, published in 1572, placed maritime expansion in a Portuguese literary frame while depending on traditions of epic shared across Europe.

Printed vernaculars helped rulers, missionaries and merchants communicate across distance, but neither Spanish nor Portuguese simply replaced local languages. Multilingual production, including Indigenous grammars and dictionaries, became central to missionary work.
Add separate publication nodes and language catalogues. Map only documented reception or printing networks, not a single “language spread” polygon dated to the initial book.

title.en: First Caribbean encounters: interpretation, place names and pilotage

records.anchorText: Guanahaní/Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and the Lesser Antilles

en: The 1492 voyage entered Caribbean societies with established names, travel and exchange. The Atlas first displays this knowledge where the expedition recorded an encounter; the journal epitome preserved by Las Casas is a mediated witness.

Local people conveyed information about neighboring islands, routes and resources, while Iberian crews assigned their own names and sometimes misunderstood what they heard. Taking people aboard under coercion and unequal translation conditions are part of the evidence.

On later crossings, mission activity and settlement made linguistic and territorial knowledge more systematic. Writings associated with Ramón Pané belong to this post-contact history of transmission, which is different from inventing an earlier word-for-word record.

Create encounter notes at independently dated stops. Give local and Iberian names with their provenance; plot route information only from its documented transmission date, and do not create a pre-voyage map of Indigenous networks.

records.anchorText: La Isabela → Santo Domingo; Caparra, Jamaica, Baracoa, Havana, St. Augustine

en: La Isabela and Santo Domingo represented different settlement attempts on Hispaniola. Caparra, the Jamaica enterprise and Baracoa mark distinct trajectories, followed by new port sites such as Havana.
In 1513 Ponce de León reached Florida on a documented Castilian expedition. In 1565 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine amid competition with the French; the fifty-year gap matters.

Caribbean towns became bases for shipping and expeditions while encomienda, disease, warfare and enslaved labor transformed their societies. African and Indigenous people helped create the port cultures that survived these shocks.

records.anchorText: Guianas and Paria → Margarita and Venezuelan coast; map workshops in Iberia and Saint-Dié

en: The voyages associated with Ojeda, Juan de la Cosa and Vespucci in 1499, and with Pinzón and Lepe soon after, added reports from northern and northeastern South America. Exact landfalls and claims of priority require caution.

Charts assembled observations from people and journeys that did not share a single itinerary. The 1500 de la Cosa map, Portuguese Cantino planisphere of 1502 and Waldseemüller map of 1507 are separate witnesses.
Pearls around Cubagua encouraged settlement and coerced labor. Naming innovations on printed maps spread more quickly than European institutions did on the ground.

en: Iberian coastal reports appeared early, but Dutch, French and British enterprises established distinct settlements and jurisdictions across the Guianas. Indigenous societies maintained exchange and authority between the settlements.
Plantations concentrated around Atlantic outlets and rivers. Maroon communities in Suriname and negotiations with Indigenous interior communities complicate simple imperial territorial fills.

The constituent colonies of British Guiana came under British control and were later combined. Claims on the Essequibo frontier and the later independence of Guyana and Suriname require additional dates.

en: Bandeiras, cattle movements and river expeditions reached different parts of interior Brazil. Portuguese activity advanced along corridors that Indigenous communities already knew and used.
Mining and pasture created competing needs for transport and labor. Captive taking, mission raids and exchange were features of this movement, as were negotiations and resistance.
Village, captaincy and province boundaries changed as administrative seats responded to population and revenue. The location of the seat does not settle the full geographic reach of its authority.

en: Settlement and sugar production made São Tomé an important early Atlantic plantation society. Portuguese elites and enslaved Africans were part of a social order that produced durable Creole communities.
The island’s position supported commerce with the African mainland and later American destinations. Its role shifted as American sugar production grew and Atlantic trading systems changed.

Later cocoa estates and contract labor brought a new phase of coerced mobility, including labor from other Portuguese territories. It should not be mapped as a continuation of one unchanged sugar system.

en: The Northwest Coast voyages form an Iberian track, but Iberian expeditions did not chart the whole Arctic, Canada or Alaska. A continental reveal needs non-Iberian evidence without pretending these were Hispanic possessions.

At documented encounters, Inuit, First Nations and other Indigenous navigators supplied guidance or testimony about coasts, rivers and seasonal ice. Early Atlantic and Hudson Bay records addressed different parts of the geography and should not inherit information from later surveys.
The mapping of the Northwest Passage involved many expeditions and Indigenous assistance; Amundsen completed a navigation in 1906. A traversed passage is not a systematic survey of all inland areas.

Florida passed to Britain in 1763 and returned to Spain in the 1780s settlement; the East–West division outlasted the first transfer. The two Floridas did not all change hands in one local process.
The Louisiana retrocession and purchase were separate legal and on-the-ground transfers. Indigenous societies and communities of mixed status negotiated presence on either side of later state lines.

records.anchorText: Seville → Sanlúcar → Atlantic ports

en: The Casa de Contratación, established in Seville in 1503, regulated personnel and shipping. The office of chief pilot and the master chart brought navigation into a system of official examination and revision.
Pilots’ reports and cosmographers’ calculations gave different kinds of testimony. The Padrón Real was revised over time; no single surviving chart is an automatic substitute for all its versions.

Licensing and convoy organization supported taxation and trade, while smugglers and competing ports exposed the limits of monopoly. Printed charts circulated knowledge beyond the officials who tried to control it.

en: The appointment of Francisco de Almeida in 1505, Diu in 1509, the conquest of Goa in 1510, Malacca in 1511 and the capture of Hormuz in 1515 created a scattered imperial network.

Ports and straits mattered because they connected existing Gujarat, Arab, East African and Southeast Asian commerce. Pass systems and naval force sought leverage over traffic, but did not close every route.

Goa acquired ecclesiastical and administrative functions while merchants and local elites negotiated the terms of Portuguese presence. Local societies and trade alternatives limited the reach of Lisbon’s system.
Show forts and sea lanes as a network, with separate layers for municipal or port jurisdiction. The 1502 Cantino plate predates most of these conquests and is background only.

en: Early Portuguese forts and markets entered an Indian Ocean system long sustained by African and Asian commerce. Ilha de Moçambique served as a staging point for routes to India.

The Zambezi settlements at Sena and Tete supported a different inland network. Prazos, African authorities and merchant communities produced forms of power that cannot all be classed as direct rule from the coast.

Gold, ivory and enslaved people moved through these corridors; local authorities could redirect trade and challenge settlers. Late-century territorial agreements and military campaigns changed the scale of colonial intervention.

records.anchorText: Urabá/Darién → Pacific; Panamá, León and Granada

en: Santa María la Antigua del Darién formed near the Gulf of Urabá in 1510. Balboa’s 1513 crossing used Indigenous knowledge and followed a route through inhabited polities.

Panamá City’s foundation in 1519 shifted the main administrative and interoceanic axis. Settlements at León and Granada in 1524 extended the network into Nicaragua; neither town should stand in for the whole region.
Isthmian crossings moved people, supplies and later silver. They also relied on forced labor and generated conflict with Indigenous societies that persisted beyond the early town foundations.
Keep Balboa as an existing route and give Darién and Panamá separate life cycles. Mark portage as a land segment and avoid using later Panama Canal geometry as the early colonial itinerary.

title.en: Portuguese Timor, sandalwood and the partition of the island

records.anchorText: Solor, Lifau, Dili, Oecusse and Dutch–Portuguese boundary

en: Portuguese traders and missionaries operated in the region before a consolidated colonial administration existed. Sandalwood commerce tied Timor to other Asian ports and gave local rulers considerable bargaining power.
Lifau and later Dili served as Portuguese seats. Topass communities and local kingdoms complicate any map with only Portuguese and Dutch colors.
Negotiation, the 1859 treaty and later agreements and arbitration established much of the partition over time. Oecusse is a visible result of the separate history of enclave and mainland districts.
Animate the trade and settlement network first. Add treaty and demarcation segments with their own dates, then link to the twentieth-century Timor-Leste record.

records.anchorText: Malacca, Banda, Ternate, Tidore, Colombo and Cochin

en: The Portuguese capture of Malacca in 1511 and voyages toward the Spice Islands inserted a new armed network into an existing Asian system. The Castilian expedition that reached Tidore encountered its own political opportunities.
The Treaty of Zaragoza in 1529 addressed rivalry over the Moluccas, but the position of its line depended on uncertain geography. Asian leaders continued to shape which Europeans could trade or stay.
Dutch victories at Malacca, in Ceylon and at Cochin rearranged ports at different dates. Maritime authority depended on shipping seasons, defense, credit and local alliances.
Track Zaragoza as a claim instrument. Show ports with governing intervals and retain independent Asian polities, especially alternating alliances at Ternate and Tidore.

records.anchorText: Río de la Plata → Paraná → Paraguay River → Asunción

en: Solís reached the estuary in 1516; Cabot’s later voyage investigated the inland river system. The estuary’s name reflected expectations of upland riches rather than a discovery of silver at its mouth.
The settlement at Buenos Aires in 1536 was abandoned; Asunción, founded in 1537, endured and became a base for further settlement. Garay re-established Buenos Aires in 1580.

Guaraní alliances and kinship ties enabled settlement and shaped the mestizo society, while forced service and conflict accompanied expansion. The waterway oriented inland trade toward multiple outlets.
Track abandonment, relocation and refounding explicitly. Different waterways should unlock at different times, and neither city’s existence justifies a fill over the Gran Chaco.

records.anchorText: Cuba → Yucatán → Gulf Coast → Veracruz → Tlaxcala → Basin of Mexico

en: The expeditions of Hernández de Córdoba and Grijalva approached the Yucatán and Gulf Coast in 1517–1518; Alonso Álvarez de Pineda’s 1519 voyage contributed a separate coastal reconnaissance.

Cortés advanced inland through alliances and armed confrontation. Indigenous interpreters and guides supplied information about roads, cities and local authorities; show those details at the encounter or recorded transmission. Tlaxcalan and other Indigenous participants were decisive in the siege that ended in August 1521, alongside epidemic disease and the disruption of supplies.

The city remained a political and economic center after conquest, but its material landscape and ruling institutions changed. Spanish knowledge of the coast, conquest of the capital and conquest of distant regions are independent questions.
Retain the existing conquest card. Add the maritime tracks, a documented inland route, and separately dated political changes; the fall of Tenochtitlan must not light all of modern Mexico.

title.en: The Iberian Atlantic slave trades and their abolition

records.anchorText: Embarkation regions in Africa → Caribbean, Brazil and mainland destinations

en: Contracted supply to Spanish America and Portuguese trafficking to Brazil connected overlapping markets. Captive people came from varied societies, and embarkation ports do not identify their ethnic origins.
Ships, credit and plantations made the trade central to Atlantic economies. Forced labor extended beyond sugar zones to towns, ranches, domestic service and mines.

Resistance included escapes, maroon settlements, shipboard action and litigation. Suppression of the Atlantic trade and the abolition of slavery were distinct and occurred at different dates across the Iberian world.

Import documented voyage data with the dataset’s attribution and uncertainty, and respect aggregate versus ship-level evidence. Build separate abolition events for each polity; 1888 is Brazil’s national abolition, not a shared imperial end date.

title.en: The global route of Magellan and Elcano as a linked log

records.anchorText: Sanlúcar → Brazilian coast → Patagonia → strait → Guam → Philippines → Moluccas → Cape → Sanlúcar

en: The fleet departed in 1519 to seek a westward passage to the Spice Islands. Its stay on the Patagonian coast and the passage of the strait in 1520 made those locations distinct geographic milestones.
The Pacific crossing exposed the distances involved and the limits of provisioning. Magellan died at Mactan in 1521 amid conflict with forces led by Lapulapu.

Elcano completed the circumnavigation aboard the Victoria in 1522 after the expedition reached the Moluccas. The route joined ocean basins without settling the competing commercial claims later handled at Zaragoza.
Keep the existing circumnavigation card and separate the ships and legs where they diverged. The 1628 strait chart is later context, not the route log.

records.anchorText: Tabasco, Veracruz/Cempoala, Tlaxcala, Cholula, Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco

en: The 1519 expedition depended on interpretation. Malintzin, also called Doña Marina, and Jerónimo de Aguilar linked speech communities in early dealings; local alliances and knowledge of routes shaped decisions long before the siege of Tenochtitlan.

Tlaxcala, Totonac communities and Mexica tributaries pursued political goals of their own. Markets, canals and roads entered Iberian testimony through encounters and texts, rather than becoming visible on the Atlas before the campaign.

Cortés’s letters, Nahua testimony assembled later and printed city views offer different perspectives. Vélez’s reading puts the coalition and its political context at the center; historians can compare it with Indigenous records and other accounts.

Start each detail at the encounter, survey or text that records it. Show later testimony and city representations with their dates and authorship; link to the retained Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco records rather than duplicating those battles or institutions.

records.anchorText: Sanlúcar → Mactan → Tidore → Cape route → Sanlúcar; Acapulco–Manila track

en: Elcano returned in 1522 after reaching the Moluccas, where the expedition dealt with Muslim rulers in a commercial and political world of their own. Bueno treats the circumnavigation as the practical realization of the globe round which the western project had been imagined.

That achievement did not place Iberian forces behind an Ottoman front in a military campaign. Zaragoza in 1529 was primarily an agreement about Iberian rivalry in the Moluccas; Manila and the repeatable Pacific route came later.

The Ottoman struggle continued on its own Mediterranean front, while Portugal dealt with changing rivals in the Indian Ocean. The contemporary events can be compared without making Tidore, Morocco, the Mamluks and the Ottomans one political unit.

Keep the existing voyage and Manila routes. Use this record as an interpretive link to Bueno and Insua, with distinct factual milestones for circumnavigation, Zaragoza, the Pacific return and Lepanto.

title.en: Epidemics and ecological change after contact

records.anchorText: Caribbean ports, Mexico, Andean cities and Brazil; regional case studies

en: Plants, animals and microbes crossed oceans through repeated sailings and local circulation. Smallpox in Mexico in the early 1520s is a documented case, but dating and diagnosis vary sharply across regions.
Introduced livestock changed land use; American crops changed diets and livelihoods elsewhere. Trade and botanical exchange did not offset the shocks of warfare, forced relocation or disease.

Demographic crises altered labor systems, political bargaining and the survival of towns. Communities also adapted and persisted, and the long-term population record cannot be reduced to a single mortality estimate.
Add outbreak and crop-transfer records at the scale warranted by each source. Keep dating ranges and competing estimates visible; an epidemic route should not create a census-like fill.

title.en: Andean guides, roads and the translation of local governance

records.anchorText: Tumbes, Cajamarca, Cusco and surveyed segments of the Qhapaq Ñan

en: Iberian reconnaissance from Panamá reached communities on the Pacific coast before the campaign into the Andes. Guides, intermediaries and existing towns helped determine how expedition parties moved and found supplies.

The existing Andean road system mattered to the march toward Cajamarca and Cusco and was repeatedly used after conquest. The Atlas shows an attested part when it enters expedition accounts or colonial surveys; construction and Atlas display dates may be centuries apart.

Quechua and other languages shaped mission, legal and administrative practice. Interpreters and Indigenous authorities helped officials navigate existing affiliations, stores and obligations, even as colonial institutions changed them.

Add a provenance note to each shown road segment and each interpretation event. Link to the Pacific route, contemporary Indigenous polities and the later survey layers; avoid a uniform road reveal triggered by the capture of one city.

title.en: Guatemala, Yucatán and the persistence of independent Petén

records.anchorText: Guatemalan highlands, Mérida, Lake Petén Itzá

en: The 1524 campaign in the Guatemalan highlands combined Indigenous allies and Spanish soldiers against existing powers. In Yucatán, campaigns and settlements proceeded through a different, prolonged chronology.
Highland towns, lowland forests and peninsular ports did not offer the same routes or resources. Mérida’s foundation in 1542 did not give effective control of inland Maya kingdoms.
The Itza capital at Nojpetén fell in 1697. Trade, missions and Indigenous mobility had connected the Petén to colonial territory without eliminating its political independence.

Split the highland, peninsular and Petén sequences. Show Nojpetén as an independent polity until locally supported changes, and label northern Guatemala’s forest frontiers over any broad audiencia claim.

title.en: Pacific coast reconnaissance and the passage into the Andes

records.anchorText: Panamá → Colombian and Ecuadorian Pacific → Tumbes → Cajamarca → Cusco → Lima

en: Expeditions from Panamá explored the Pacific South American coast in stages before the Spanish entered the Andes. Tumbes and coastal encounters belong to an itinerary quite distinct from the road to Cajamarca.
Atahualpa’s capture in 1532 took place after an Inca civil war. Cusco’s occupation did not end Inca resistance or determine the eventual boundaries of the Viceroyalty of Peru.
Lima’s foundation in 1535 connected the new capital to maritime supply. Indigenous road systems, alliances and existing political divisions made the movement of people and resources possible.
Cross-link the existing Andes and New Laws cards. Add coastal reconnaissance, Lima, Cusco and the Vilcabamba resistance, which ended as a state center in 1572.

records.anchorText: Coro, Maracaibo, Santa Marta → Magdalena → Bogotá plateau

en: The Welser concession set up a distinct enterprise around Venezuela beginning in 1528. Searches for wealth and passage led to repeated inland journeys, not uniform control across the Llanos.

Quesada’s expedition moved up the Magdalena toward Muisca lands; rival expeditions reached the plateau by other routes. Santa Fe became an administrative node, and an audiencia was created in the mid-sixteenth century.
Ports and river valleys connected highland production and trade to the Caribbean. Muisca communities, other Indigenous societies and African labor were central to the region’s new economy.

Add concessions, routes and seats separately. Keep Orinoco tributaries and the Guianas dark on the specific Iberian chart layer unless a named chart attests them; no generalized Venezuela-to-Amazon fill.

en: The Narváez disaster produced a long overland journey by Cabeza de Vaca and other survivors. De Soto’s expedition crossed the Mississippi in 1541; Coronado’s expedition reached Plains communities by another corridor.

Cabrillo’s 1542–1543 voyage surveyed portions of the Pacific coast from New Spain. The three inland itineraries and the coastal voyage have different evidence and should not be joined by a guessed connecting line.

Indigenous towns gave expedition parties supplies, passage or resistance. Expedition reports entered later cartography, but these journeys did not create permanent settlements across the Southeast or Plains.
Use alternative tracks for disputed sites and attach primary narratives by leg. At continental scale reveal corridors, not U.S. states or whole watersheds.

records.anchorText: Southern Plains and New Mexico–Texas trade corridors

en: Coronado and other expeditions transited some Plains corridors, while much later surveys recorded other parts. Neither process made the interior empty or politically fixed.
Comanche power shaped exchange, tribute, diplomacy and violence across a region whose reach varied over time. Spanish, Mexican and U.S. authorities dealt with it under changing conditions.
Treaties transferred claims between states without eliminating Indigenous power. Subsequent military campaigns, treaty-making, removal and reservations added separate layers of governance.
Avoid a false continuous Spanish fill across the Plains. Use dated nodes, contested zones and distance-appropriate route confidence to show both trade and jurisdiction.

records.anchorText: Guadalajara → Zacatecas → Durango → Santa Bárbara → upper Río Grande

en: Northern expeditions and settlements connected the western Mexican interior with silver centers. Zacatecas’s growth after the silver finds of 1546 was distinct from the founding of the civil and judicial seats administering it.
Roads, presidios and towns protected movement in some corridors and exposed travelers in others. Chichimeca resistance and negotiated settlements shaped the route over decades.
Silver moved labor, livestock, credit and supplies north and south. Indigenous alliances, migration and the establishment of Tlaxcalan settlements made certain corridors more durable.

records.anchorText: São Vicente, Pernambuco, Salvador, Guanabara

en: São Vicente, founded in 1532, marked a turn toward permanent settlement. Hereditary captaincies divided administrative grants along the coast without fixing the poorly defined western reach of each grant.
The general government at Salvador began in 1549. Coastal sugar zones, mission villages and port cities developed unevenly; some captaincies struggled to sustain settlers.

French settlement in Guanabara challenged Portuguese authority and depended on Indigenous allies, as did Portuguese resistance. Rio de Janeiro was founded in 1565 and rival positions were defeated in 1567.
Import grants as hatched schematic claims with uncertain inland extents. Put mills, missions, Salvador and Rio on their own layers and allow competing claims near Guanabara.

records.anchorText: Mexico City, printing workshop, university and diocesan seats

en: Antonio de Mendoza’s appointment in 1535 established viceregal government around an existing city, audiencia and municipal network. These institutions exercised different powers and did not all cover the same area.

A press began operating in Mexico City in 1539. The university was authorized in 1551 and opened in 1553; manuscript painting, translation and Indigenous-language printing continued alongside Castilian texts.

Urban institutions trained clergy and officials and supplied information to the monarchy. They also created forums where Indigenous elites, religious orders and officials advanced competing accounts of tribute and rights.
Keep the current Mendoza card and add institution points with activation dates. Separate an education and language layer from any change in territorial authority.

en: The Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco opened in 1536 as a center for the education of Indigenous elites. Nahua scholars worked within and beyond the institutional priorities of Franciscans and officials.

The Florentine Codex is a product of Indigenous knowledge and collaborative textual work, with Nahuatl and Spanish columns and an extensive visual record. Bernardino de Sahagún should be named alongside the Indigenous collaborators.
The project documented history, speech, plants, trades and religious life amid profound change. Its material survival preserves perspectives that official maps and decrees cannot supply.
Map the school and production site; link manuscript books, folios and named people as separate objects. Do not present manuscript migration as a contemporary publication route without evidence.

records.anchorText: Salamanca → Valladolid → Madrid; case-study links to the Indies

en: Vitoria’s 1539 lectures treated Indigenous peoples as holders of political and property rights and examined proposed titles to rule. The Valladolid debate later made disagreement over conquest and evangelization visible at court.

Legal argument moved among universities, religious orders, tribunals and American communities. Royal measures restricted some abuses and preserved other forms of compulsory labor; legal texts need evidence of how they were applied.
The 1680 Recopilación collected orders produced over generations. Its categories expose the range of institutions, from audiencias to local authorities and communities, within the composite monarchy.

Retain the existing legal milestones and add linked records for Vitoria and the Recopilación. Display law and jurisdiction with legal-source citations; never infer effective borders from a protection or a debate.

en: Santiago’s foundation in 1541 began a colonial town network in central Chile. Expansion south met Mapuche resistance and did not produce continuous control over the zone between central Chile and Chiloé.

The crisis following Curalaba in 1598 destroyed or forced withdrawal from several settlements. The 1641 Parliament of Quillín illustrates negotiated relations, with continuing disputes over interpretation and outcomes.
Forts, agriculture and livestock sustained frontier economies. Political and commercial dealings across the Biobío persisted even when settlement and military advances failed.
Use dated towns and forts, including closures. Render a frontier zone and Mapuche autonomy where evidence supports it; do not style Quillín as if it were a modern surveyed boundary.

en: The New Laws of 1542 addressed Indigenous enslavement and encomienda abuses and created a new framework for government. The Peruvian viceroyalty and the conflicts over enforcement developed in stages.
Potosí’s silver boom after 1545 reshaped routes into the high Andes. Viceroy Toledo’s reforms linked mining to mercury supply, forced draft labor and resettlement.
Silver supported urban life and transoceanic exchange while making Indigenous communities bear heavy costs. Legal protections and labor coercion coexisted within the same monarchy.
Separate legislation, installation of government and realized control. Add mining nodes and changing supply routes; avoid treating a vice-regal outline as the area that Potosí directly governed.

records.anchorText: Tanegashima, Nagasaki, Macao and Portuguese transit ports

en: Portuguese merchants entered Japanese trade in the mid-sixteenth century. Their shipping intersected with Chinese commerce and routes running through Macao.

Francis Xavier arrived in 1549, and Catholic missions developed under differing local authorities. The politics of Japanese unification eventually changed the terms on which those missions and traders could function.
Macao–Nagasaki traffic helped finance wider networks. Expulsion of Portuguese traders in 1639 and survival of Christian communities were separate developments.
Show trade edges and missionary sites with independent intervals. Japanese sovereignty is never replaced along the shipping line; the Macao plan is a contextual image of one terminus.

en: The date 1557 conventionally marks durable Portuguese settlement at Macao. Its role developed through accommodation with Chinese officials, and its early legal status should not be read backward from later treaties.

Macao connected South China to Japan, Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean. Merchants, missionaries, interpreters and shipping networks made it a transit point rather than a territorial route through China.

The 1887 treaty changed the legal vocabulary surrounding Portuguese occupation and administration. The 1999 transfer belongs to a separate modern entry and does not retroactively settle earlier categories.
Add a port node, trade edges and later boundary instruments where sourced. The 1781 plate is a town plan only; it depicts neither the initial agreement nor the modern special administrative region.

en: Officials asked towns to describe geography, population, resources and custom. In the late sixteenth century responses to the Relaciones geográficas program included maps made with different local conventions.
Indigenous painters and knowledge holders supplied many descriptions, and maps recorded routes, rivers, places and contested pasts that could not be read from European coastal charts.
The questionnaires helped officials understand tribute and geography, but surviving returns are uneven. Some describe local landscapes in depth and others barely locate them.

Link images and responses at the town level, with author and date where known. Overlay only georeferenced material suitable for comparison; do not color unsurveyed spaces because an answer exists nearby.

en: Legazpi’s expedition reached the Philippines in 1565. Urdaneta’s return via northern Pacific latitudes established a route that could be repeated; document Alonso de Arellano’s earlier arrival in New Spain separately.
Manila became a Spanish colonial seat in 1571 on a site with prior settlements and regional ties. Acapulco connected the Pacific exchange to New Spain’s land and Atlantic routes.
American silver moved west while Asian goods and people moved east. Chinese merchants, Filipino shipbuilders, seafarers and Mexican intermediaries sustained the network.

records.anchorText: Callao → Solomon Islands; Marquesas and Santa Cruz; Espiritu Santo → Torres Strait

en: Mendaña’s first expedition reached the Solomon Islands in 1568, and the second reached the Marquesas and Santa Cruz in 1595. They drew on Peruvian ports and expectations of Pacific trade and settlement.
Quirós reached Espiritu Santo in 1606. Torres followed a separate course past New Guinea through the strait that now bears his name.

Brief settlement attempts, conflict, illness and a dispersed command structure limited the expeditions’ outcomes. The resulting reports were not equivalent to immediately usable European charts of every island passed.
Create three voyage objects with separate actors and endpoints; give each leg its own source. Show local navigation only when documented in encounters or later exchanges.

title.en: Lepanto, the Armada and the maritime limits of Spanish power

records.anchorText: Gulf of Patras/Lepanto; Lisbon, English Channel and the return around Britain and Ireland

en: At Lepanto in 1571 a Holy League fleet defeated Ottoman forces. It was a major Mediterranean battle without an automatic change of sovereignty across the sea.
The Armada of 1588 pursued a different strategy against England, dependent on coordination with forces in the Low Countries. Naval action, weather and logistics all shaped its failure.

The two campaigns illuminate different coalitions and technologies as well as a monarchy balancing the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Neither battle establishes that one empire thereafter controlled all surrounding waters.
Show two separate campaign tracks with loss locations and confidence where documented. Use an overview card as connective tissue without joining Lepanto and the Armada into one continuous route.

records.anchorText: Selected towns in Mexico, Andes and Brazil

en: The 1573 ordinances on discovery, settlement and pacification prescribed aspects of town foundation. Older settlements and local planning practices cannot all be derived from legislation issued later.

Plazas, churches, roads and markets linked institutions to directed movement through urban space. Resettlement programs could bring services and ecclesiastical organization while dispossessing communities of older sites.

Baroque public culture acquired locally distinctive forms, carried by Indigenous and Afro-descendant artisans as well as religious orders and patrons. Luso-American towns had their own institutional and architectural histories.
Show town plans at local zoom and record relocation as an event. Cross-link the printed law, surviving plans and material sites without extrapolating a single city model across both empires.

records.anchorText: Luanda, Kwanza corridor, Benguela, Ndongo and Matamba

en: Paulo Dias de Novais established the Portuguese settlement at Luanda in the 1570s. Other African polities and ports retained distinct sovereignties and pursued diplomacy and war with competing partners.
Njinga’s career exposes the limits of describing the interior as an extension of Luanda. The Dutch occupied Luanda in 1641; a Portuguese expedition organized from Brazil recovered it in 1648.

The slave trade tied Angola closely to Brazil, while coercion and war broke up some communities and enabled others to consolidate. Religion and diplomacy served African as well as Portuguese political goals.
Animate separate episodes for port control and for inland campaigns. A commercial route to a market is not a corridor of Portuguese sovereignty.

title.en: Composite monarchy under the Iberian Union and its rupture

records.anchorText: Lisbon, Tomar, Madrid; inset ports across both monarchies

en: Philip’s succession and the Cortes of Tomar put the crowns under one monarch while Portuguese laws, offices and institutions retained a distinct footing.
European wars had consequences overseas, where ports faced Dutch attacks as rivals targeted Iberian trade. Sharing a sovereign did not turn Brazil, Angola or Goa into provinces of Castile.

Portugal’s restoration in 1640 and Spanish recognition in 1668 were separate political thresholds. Overseas actors did not respond everywhere on the same day, and Ceuta followed a different trajectory.
Preserve the existing union and restoration milestones. Use a common sovereign field over independently rendered administrations and model wartime port changes on a separate layer.

records.anchorText: Cortés’s Gulf crossings → Loreto → Baja missions; Sonora and Pimería Alta inset

en: Sixteenth-century expeditions tested the coast and Gulf of California. Disagreement in later maps over California as peninsula or island shows why charting should advance unevenly and sometimes display error.
Loreto’s permanent mission dates to 1697. Jesuit, Franciscan and Dominican phases affected individual sites differently, and nearby Indigenous societies retained knowledge and agency.
Mission networks depended on supplies from across the gulf and distinct Sonoran connections. Secularization and later national settlement did not occur uniformly across the peninsula.
Add Baja separately from Alta California; keep early attempts and mission relocations distinct. Use the 1562 plate or other period maps to show representation rather than override surveyed geography.

records.anchorText: El Paso → Ohkay Owingeh/San Juan → Santa Fe and Pueblo towns

en: Oñate’s 1598 expedition extended settlement along the upper Río Grande. Santa Fe became a capital in the early seventeenth century, while Pueblo towns remained distinct communities.
Missions and ranching brought opportunities and coercion, including demands on labor and religious conflict. Acoma’s resistance and subsequent punishment deserve separate treatment.
In 1680 Pueblo forces expelled Spanish authorities from much of New Mexico. Diego de Vargas’s return in 1692–1693 involved both negotiations and renewed warfare.
